meta.title: Who really said "I shall return"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: MacArthur really said it, at Terowie, South Australia, on 20 March 1942. The Advertiser printed his full words: "I came through and I shall return."
meta.ogDescription: Genuine MacArthur. The Advertiser (Adelaide) printed his words on 21 March 1942: "I came through and I shall return." It is not "I came out of Bataan."

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: MacArthur spoke it to reporters at Terowie, South Australia, on 20 March 1942, after his escape from the Philippines. The Advertiser (Adelaide) printed his statement on its front page the next day, ending: “I came through and I shall return.” A scan of that page confirms the wording.

source.excerpt: “The President of the United States ordered me to break through the Japanese lines and proceed from Corregidor to Australia for the purpose, as I understand it, of organising an American offensive against Japan, the primary purpose of which is the relief of the Philippines. I came through and I shall return.”
trail: The printed record. The Advertiser (Adelaide) ran the statement on its front page under the headline “I Came Through; I Shall Return” (page scan on Wikimedia Commons ↗).

Place and date. Wikipedia places the statement at Terowie, South Australia, on 20 March 1942, cites the same Advertiser page, and notes it is often misquoted as “I came out of Bataan and I shall return” (Wikipedia ↗).

Wikiquote. MacArthur’s Wikiquote page lists the line as “I came out of Bataan and I shall return!” (Terowie, 20 March 1942) and flags it as needing a specific citation (Wikiquote ↗). The 1942 newspaper text reads “I came through.”

The promise kept. The FDR Presidential Library’s blog quotes “I came through and I shall return” and describes the Leyte landing of 20 October 1944, where his speech opened “People of the Philippines: I have returned” (National Archives FDR blog ↗).
source.excerptNote: As printed in The Advertiser (Adelaide), 21 March 1942, p. 1, with the paper’s spelling “organising.” The paper adds that MacArthur first asked whether his message would reach the United States.

source.rightsNote: The words were first published on 21 March 1942 in The Advertiser (Adelaide). That is after the 1931 cutoff, so quotle.info conservatively treats the statement as in copyright, held by MacArthur’s estate. This holds even though Wikimedia Commons marks its scan of the newspaper page as public domain. Quoting a short line for commentary is ordinary fair use.

author.name: Douglas MacArthur
author.heading: About Douglas MacArthur
author.metaLine: 1880–1964 · American general, Supreme Commander of the Southwest Pacific Area
author.bio: Douglas MacArthur (26 January 1880 – 5 April 1964) was an American general. He served as Chief of Staff of the U.S. Army, as Supreme Commander of the Southwest Pacific Area in the Second World War, and later led the occupation of Japan and the UN Command in Korea. In March 1942 he was ordered out of the Philippines to Australia. He promised to come back, and he did so in October 1944, when he landed on Leyte.

misattribution.heading: The versions that get passed around
misattribution.intro: No one else is credited with the line. MacArthur really said it. The trouble is the wording that gets attached to it.

items.who: “I came out of Bataan and I shall return!”
items.why: This is the most common reworded version, and Wikiquote lists it with a citation-needed flag. Wikipedia calls it a frequent misquotation. The 1942 newspaper text says “I came through,” and MacArthur’s statement describes leaving from Corregidor (Wikipedia ↗).

Wikipedia says the Filipino journalist Carlos Romulo first suggested “We shall return,” and that the Office of War Information later proposed the plural. MacArthur refused to change it (Wikipedia ↗). The FDR Library blog says the White House asked for the change and he refused (FDR blog ↗).
People sometimes mix up the two lines. “I have returned” is a different statement, made on Leyte on 20 October 1944, more than two years after Terowie (History.com ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The documented wording is “I came through and I shall return,” spoken at Terowie and printed in The Advertiser (Adelaide) on 21 March 1942 (page scan ↗).

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: MacArthur had been ordered off Corregidor while American and Filipino troops were still fighting on Bataan. When he reached Terowie he had already been in Australia for several days. The Advertiser reported that this was his first interview with the press, and that he first asked whether his message would reach the United States.
He turned the closing clause into a personal pledge to the Philippines. He kept it on 20 October 1944, when he landed on Leyte and told the Filipino people by radio, “I have returned.”
